chapter_title: Direct Connect Gateways and Global Connectivity
chapter_summary:
As your AWS footprint expands across multiple regions, managing hybrid connectivity can become increasingly complex. If you were to rely solely on individual Private VIFs connected to Virtual Private Gateways (VGWs), you would need a separate Direct Connect connection (or at least a separate VIF) for each region where you have VPCs. This approach quickly becomes unwieldy, costly, and difficult to manage. This is precisely the problem that **AWS Direct Connect Gateway** solves. A Direct Connect Gateway acts as a globally available resource that allows you to connect your on-premises network to multiple VPCs across different AWS regions using a single Direct Connect connection. It's a game-changer for organizations operating a global AWS presence.

The core benefit of a Direct Connect Gateway is its ability to centralize your hybrid connectivity. Instead of having point-to-point connections to each regional VGW, you establish a single Private VIF (or Transit VIF) to the Direct Connect Gateway. This gateway then allows you to associate multiple VGWs (each attached to a VPC in a different region) or Transit Gateways (TGWs) with it. This creates a flexible, many-to-one or many-to-many routing architecture. For example, with a single Direct Connect connection in `us-east-1` and a Direct Connect Gateway, you can connect to VPCs in `us-east-1`, `us-west-2`, `eu-central-1`, and `ap-southeast-2` simultaneously. This significantly reduces the operational overhead and cost associated with managing multiple physical DX connections or VIFs.

When you create a Direct Connect Gateway, you give it a name and specify a unique Amazon-side ASN (Autonomous System Number). This ASN is used for BGP peering between your on-premises router and the Direct Connect Gateway. After the gateway is created, you associate it with one or more VGWs or TGWs. It's important to note that a VGW must be attached to a VPC before it can be associated with a Direct Connect Gateway. Similarly, a TGW must have VPC attachments before it can be associated. Once associated, your on-premises network can exchange routes with all the VPCs connected via those VGWs/TGWs. The routing table of your on-premises router will learn the CIDR blocks of all associated VPCs, and the route tables of your VPCs will learn your on-premises CIDRs.

```bash
# Example AWS CLI command to create a Direct Connect Gateway
aws directconnect create-direct-connect-gateway \
    --direct-connect-gateway-name "MyGlobalDXGateway" \
    --amazon-side-asn 64512 \
    --region us-east-1 # DX Gateway is a global resource, but managed from a region

# Example AWS CLI command to associate a VGW with a DX Gateway
aws directconnect associate-virtual-gateway \
    --direct-connect-gateway-id dxgw-abcdefgh \
    --virtual-gateway-id vgw-1234567890abcdef0 \
    --region us-east-1 # VGW is regional, so specify its region
```
These commands demonstrate the creation of a Direct Connect Gateway and the association of a regional VGW with it. The `amazon-side-asn` for the DX Gateway can be any private ASN (64512-65534).

There are crucial routing considerations and limitations when working with Direct Connect Gateways. First, **overlapping CIDR blocks are not allowed** across any of the associated VPCs or between your on-premises network and the associated VPCs. This is a fundamental networking principle, but it's especially critical to enforce with a Direct Connect Gateway to prevent routing conflicts. Second, **transitive routing is not supported** through a Direct Connect Gateway. This means that traffic from one associated VGW/VPC cannot directly reach another associated VGW/VPC through the Direct Connect Gateway. The traffic must always flow from the on-premises network to the target VPC. If you need VPC-to-VPC communication across regions via your hybrid connection, you would typically use a Transit Gateway attached to the Direct Connect Gateway, or separate inter-region VPC peering/TGW peering. Third, the Direct Connect Gateway itself does not perform NAT (Network Address Translation). All communication is based on private IP addresses.

For advanced global connectivity, pairing a Direct Connect Gateway with **AWS Transit Gateway** offers the most robust and scalable solution. You can attach a Transit Gateway to a Direct Connect Gateway using a Transit VIF. This allows your on-premises network to connect to the Transit Gateway, which then acts as a central hub for all your VPCs (and other TGW attachments like VPNs) across multiple regions. This architecture provides a truly global network backbone, simplifying routing, enhancing security, and enabling complex network topologies. When using TGW with DX Gateway, the TGW's route tables manage the routing between the on-premises network and the various VPCs attached to the TGW. This is the recommended pattern for large-scale, multi-region, multi-account hybrid cloud deployments.

Common mistakes include forgetting to update VPC route tables to point to the VGW (or TGW) for on-premises routes, or not properly configuring BGP on the on-premises router to advertise the correct prefixes to the Direct Connect Gateway. Remember that the Direct Connect Gateway is a global resource, but the VGWs and TGWs you associate with it are regional. Ensure your BGP configuration on your on-premises router is robust enough to handle route advertisements from all associated VPCs and that you apply appropriate route filtering if necessary.

screens.title: Direct Connect Gateways and Global Connectivity
screens.subtitle: Centralize hybrid connections to reach multiple AWS regions from a single Direct Connect point

narration.text: In this lesson we will explore the AWS Direct Connect Gateway and why it matters when your cloud footprint spans multiple regions. You will learn how a single Direct Connect connection can be turned into a global hybrid entry point, how Virtual Private Gateways and Transit Gateways attach, and what routing rules you must respect to avoid conflicts. I'll use concrete examples so you can picture a single connection in one region supporting VPCs in many others without creating dozens of physical connections. We'll also cover the practical steps for creating the gateway, assigning an Amazon-side ASN for BGP peering, and associating regional VGWs or TGWs. Importantly, you will understand the limitations: overlapping CIDRs are not allowed and Direct Connect Gateways do not forward traffic transitively between associated VGWs. Those two points often surprise learners, so we'll highlight them and show how attaching a Transit Gateway can provide the global hub many enterprises need. By the end you'll be able to explain the architecture, outline the configuration steps, and reason about route advertisement and route table changes in a multi-region hybrid architecture.

keyIdea.text: A Direct Connect Gateway centralizes hybrid connectivity so one Direct Connect connection can reach multiple regional VPCs via associated VGWs or TGWs.

screens.title: Why Direct Connect Gateway exists
screens.subtitle: The problem of scaling hybrid connections and the DX Gateway solution

narration.text: When organizations expand to multiple AWS regions, hybrid connectivity quickly becomes operationally heavy if you rely on one private virtual interface per region. Imagine provisioning a separate Direct Connect connection or VIF for every region where you run VPCs — each connection needs its own configuration, BGP session, and monitoring. The Direct Connect Gateway was designed to solve that exact problem by acting as a global attachment point. It lets you establish a single Private VIF or Transit VIF to the Direct Connect Gateway and then associate many regional Virtual Private Gateways or Transit Gateways. That means one physical or logical connection in a supported location can provide connectivity to VPCs in many regions. A concrete example: with a Direct Connect in us-east-1 and a Direct Connect Gateway, you can reach VPCs in us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-central-1, and ap-southeast-2 without separate VIFs per region. A common misconception is thinking a DX Gateway forwards traffic between VPCs directly; it does not. Its role is to centralize the hybrid entry point and exchange routes between on-premises and the associated regional gateways. The main takeaway is that a Direct Connect Gateway reduces cost and complexity while requiring careful route planning across regions.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Direct Connect Gateway centralizes a hybrid entry point so a single Direct Connect can serve VPCs in many regions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Why Direct Connect Gateway exists
Problem: scale and cost

One VIF per region multiplies management work and costs when you operate globally.

Analogy

Think of the Direct Connect Gateway as an airport hub. Instead of separate roads into every city, flights land at one hub and passengers connect to regional carriers.

Concrete example

A single connection in us-east-1 with a DX Gateway can reach VPCs in us-west-2 and eu-central-1 via associated VGWs.

Key Takeaway

DX Gateway centralizes connectivity so you maintain a single hybrid entry point for many regions.

Definition and quick facts
  • Global resource managed from a region but usable across regions.
  • Works with Private VIFs or Transit VIFs to reach VGWs or TGWs.
  • Requires BGP peering using an Amazon-side ASN you choose.
Common misconception

A Direct Connect Gateway does not enable VPC-to-VPC transit between associated VGWs. Traffic must go to or from on-premises unless a Transit Gateway is used.

screens.title: Create and configure a Direct Connect Gateway
screens.subtitle: Naming, Amazon-side ASN and preparing BGP peering

narration.text: Creating a Direct Connect Gateway is a straightforward process but each step has operational significance. First, you choose a friendly name for management and audit purposes. Then you specify an Amazon-side Autonomous System Number, typically from the private ASN range such as 64512–65534. The Amazon-side ASN becomes the ASN used by AWS for BGP sessions and will be presented to your on-premises router during peering. Remember that the DX Gateway is managed from a specific region, even though the resource is global. After creation, you create a Private VIF or Transit VIF on your Direct Connect connection to that gateway. That VIF terminates to the Direct Connect Gateway and begins the BGP exchange. A concrete command-line example to create a Direct Connect Gateway looks like the following code block, managed from a region like us-east-1. After creation, verify BGP neighbor details and ensure your on-premises router advertises the correct prefixes and accepts the Amazon-side ASN. A common mistake is picking an ASN that collides with your on-premises ASN space or failing to allow the ASN in your routing policies. Always validate BGP sessions and prefix advertisement filters as part of setup.

keyIdea.title: Action
keyIdea.text: Create the DX Gateway with a name and Amazon-side ASN, then establish a Private or Transit VIF and complete BGP peering.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Create DX Gateway
Step-by-step
  1. Create Direct Connect Gateway and set a name.
  2. Choose an Amazon-side ASN (private range 64512–65534).
  3. Create a Private VIF or Transit VIF to the DX Gateway.
  4. Complete BGP peering between on-premises router and DX Gateway.
CLI Example
aws directconnect create-direct-connect-gateway \
    --direct-connect-gateway-name "MyGlobalDXGateway" \
    --amazon-side-asn 64512 \
    --region us-east-1
Checks and validations
  • Verify the DX Gateway appears in the console and note the Amazon-side ASN.
  • Confirm the VIF is linked to the DX Gateway and BGP sessions are established.
  • Ensure on-premises router advertises intended prefixes and accepts routes from AWS.
Pitfall

Do not select an ASN that conflicts with your on-premises ASN policies; validate routing filters to avoid unwanted advertisements.

screens.title: Associating VGWs and TGWs
screens.subtitle: How to connect regional gateways to the Direct Connect Gateway

narration.text: Associating regional Virtual Private Gateways or Transit Gateways with a Direct Connect Gateway is the step that gives your on-premises network reach into remote VPCs. Before association, ensure the VGW is attached to its VPC and that a TGW has the required VPC attachments. From the DX Gateway, you create an association pointing to the VGW or TGW identifier and specify the region of the target gateway. Once associated, the Direct Connect Gateway and the regional gateway exchange route information with your on-premises router via BGP. An important operational point: a VGW must be attached to its VPC before you can associate it with the DX Gateway; similarly, TGWs must have their VPC attachments in place. A concrete command to associate a VGW looks like the CLI example shown in the lesson. After association, validate that your on-premises router learns the VPC CIDR prefixes and that the VPCs’ route tables point back to their VGW or TGW for on-premises destinations. A common mistake is attempting association before attachments exist, which will result in configuration errors. Always verify attachments first and then associate.

keyIdea.title: Association
keyIdea.text: Associate a VGW or TGW only after it has required attachments; then routes propagate via BGP to on-premises.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Associating VGWs and TGWs
Required preconditions
  • VGW must be attached to its VPC before association.
  • TGW must have VPC attachments before associating with DX Gateway.
  • Know the region of each VGW/TGW so you specify the correct region for association.
CLI Example
aws directconnect associate-virtual-gateway \
    --direct-connect-gateway-id dxgw-abcdefgh \
    --virtual-gateway-id vgw-1234567890abcdef0 \
    --region us-east-1
Validation checklist
  1. Confirm association status in the console or via CLI.
  2. Verify on-premises router learns the VPC CIDRs through BGP.
  3. Confirm each VPC route table returns on-premises traffic to the VGW or TGW.
Tip

Use route filters and BGP prefix limits to protect your on-premises routing table from unexpected advertisements.

screens.title: How routing flows with a Direct Connect Gateway
screens.subtitle: Route advertisement, learning, and return-path requirements

narration.text: Understanding routing is critical when using a Direct Connect Gateway. The on-premises router establishes a BGP session with the Direct Connect Gateway using the Amazon-side ASN. During BGP, your on-premises router advertises your corporate prefixes to AWS. The Direct Connect Gateway then shares these routes with each associated VGW or TGW so VPCs know how to reach on-premises resources. Conversely, AWS advertises VPC CIDR prefixes back to your on-premises router, so your router learns routes to every associated VPC. For traffic to correctly return to on-premises, each VPC must have route table entries pointing to its VGW or TGW for the relevant on-premises prefixes. A common oversight is configuring the DX Gateway and BGP but forgetting to update VPC route tables, which leaves packets without a valid return path. Also note that the Direct Connect Gateway itself does not perform NAT; it operates at routing level using private IP addressing. A concrete example: if your on-premises advertises 10.0.0.0/8 and a VPC advertises 10.1.0.0/16, the on-premises router must accept the VPC prefix and the VPC route table must send 10.0.0.0/8 to the VGW or TGW. Always validate both advertisement and route table state.

keyIdea.title: Routing behavior
keyIdea.text: BGP exchanges advertise VPC CIDRs to on-premises and on-premises CIDRs to VPCs; VPC route tables must point back to VGW/TGW for return traffic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Routing with DX Gateway
Routing sequence
  1. On-prem advertises corporate prefixes via BGP to the DX Gateway.
  2. DX Gateway shares on-prem prefixes with associated VGWs/TGWs.
  3. VGWs/TGWs propagate these routes to their VPC route tables.
  4. VPCs advertise their CIDRs back through VGWs/TGWs to DX Gateway and on-prem.
Concrete scenario

If on-premises advertises 10.0.0.0/8 and a VPC has 10.1.0.0/16, ensure VPC route table points 10.0.0.0/8 to its VGW so return traffic flows correctly.

Checks
  • Verify BGP adjacency status and learned prefixes on your router.
  • Confirm each VPC route table has a route to on-prem via VGW or TGW.
  • Remember DX Gateway does not perform NAT; routing must use private addresses.
Key Takeaway

Routing depends on BGP advertisements both ways and correct VPC route tables for return paths.

screens.title: Overlapping CIDRs and why they’re forbidden
screens.subtitle: Preventing routing conflicts across associated VPCs and on-premises networks

narration.text: A foundational rule when using a Direct Connect Gateway is that overlapping CIDR blocks are not allowed across any associated VPCs or between your on-premises network and those VPCs. Overlapping addresses create ambiguous routing: if two VPCs or a VPC and on-premises network share the same prefix, neither AWS nor your routers can deterministically forward traffic to the intended destination. This is not a DX-specific constraint; it's a general networking principle amplified in multi-region hybrid setups. In practice, enforce a clear addressing plan across accounts and regions before you associate VGWs or TGWs. A useful operational habit is to maintain a central IP allocation registry that prevents overlaps and documents prefixes used by each VPC. A common misconception is thinking that route filters or BGP manipulation will safely mask overlaps; while filters can block advertisements, they do not resolve the underlying addressing collision. The correct action is to redesign prefixes so they are unique. The takeaway: verify every VPC CIDR and on-premises prefix for uniqueness before association to avoid routing conflicts and service disruptions. Overlapping CIDRs and why they’re forbidden means never associate vpcs or on-premises networks with overlapping cidr blocks to a direct connect gateway.. In practical terms, preventing routing conflicts across associated vpcs and on-premises networks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Rule
keyIdea.text: Never associate VPCs or on-premises networks with overlapping CIDR blocks to a Direct Connect Gateway.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Overlapping CIDRs
Why overlaps break routing

If two networks advertise the same prefix, routers cannot choose a single correct next hop for that prefix, creating black holes or unpredictable behavior.

Operational advice

Keep a central IP registry, and validate prefixes in inventory before associating with a DX Gateway.

Misconception

Don’t assume route filters can safely resolve overlaps — the correct fix is unique addressing.

Quick checklist
  • Inventory VPC CIDRs in every region and account.
  • Compare on-premises prefixes against VPC CIDRs for overlaps.
  • Remediate overlaps by readdressing or using distinct subnets.
Key Takeaway

Unique addressing is mandatory when associating resources to a DX Gateway.

screens.title: Transitive routing limitation
screens.subtitle: What you can and cannot do with traffic between associated VGWs

narration.text: A frequent source of confusion is whether the Direct Connect Gateway allows VPC-to-VPC traffic between two VGWs simply because they’re both associated with the same gateway. The explicit rule is that transitive routing is not supported through a Direct Connect Gateway. That means if VPC-A in us-east-1 and VPC-B in eu-west-1 are both associated via their VGWs, traffic will not flow directly from VPC-A to VPC-B through the DX Gateway. The gateway exchanges routes between on-premises and each associated gateway, but it does not forward traffic from one associated VGW to another. The practical consequence is that VPC-to-VPC communication across regions requires a different mechanism: either a Transit Gateway that manages inter-VPC routing, TGW peering, or inter-region VPC peering. A concrete contrast: with TGW attached to the DX Gateway, the TGW can manage routing between VPCs and between VPCs and on-premises; without TGW, DX Gateway only connects on-premises to VPCs. A common misconception is assuming the DX Gateway creates a global fabric for arbitrary inter-VPC traffic; it does not. Always design for explicit VPC-to-VPC connectivity when needed. Transitive routing limitation means direct connect gateways do not support transitive routing between associated vgws; use tgw or peering for vpc-to-vpc communication.. In practical terms, what you can and cannot do with traffic between associated vgws. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Limitation
keyIdea.text: Direct Connect Gateways do not support transitive routing between associated VGWs; use TGW or peering for VPC-to-VPC communication.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Transitive Routing
Direct Connect Gateway

Exchanges routes between on-premises and each associated gateway but does not forward traffic between associated VGWs.

Example

Traffic from EC2 in VPC-A to EC2 in VPC-B will not traverse the DX Gateway if both VGWs are merely associated; it must take another path.

When to use TGW

Attach a Transit Gateway to DX Gateway with a Transit VIF to enable hub-and-spoke inter-VPC routing across regions.

Comparative table
DX Gateway
No transitive VPC-to-VPC routing
DX Gateway + TGW
TGW route tables manage inter-VPC and on-prem routing
Takeaway

Plan for TGW or peering if you need direct VPC-to-VPC flows across regions via your hybrid connection.

screens.title: Pairing DX Gateway with Transit Gateway
screens.subtitle: How Transit Gateway extends DX Gateway capabilities for global routing

narration.text: For advanced global connectivity, pairing a Direct Connect Gateway with an AWS Transit Gateway gives you a powerful and scalable hub. The Transit Gateway, when attached to a Direct Connect Gateway via a Transit VIF, becomes the central routing plane for many VPCs and VPNs across regions. The TGW route tables then manage how traffic moves between VPC attachments and between VPCs and on-premises. This arrangement overcomes the DX Gateway’s transitive routing limitation because the TGW performs the routing between VPC attachments. In a typical deployment, you associate the TGW with the DX Gateway and ensure the TGW has VPC attachments in regions where you need inter-VPC connectivity. BGP runs between on-premises and the DX Gateway, and the DX Gateway hands off routes to the TGW which implements the required inter-VPC routing. An operational tip: ensure TGW route tables are correctly configured and that route propagation to/from TGW is enabled for attachments you want reachable from on-premises. This architecture is recommended for large-scale, multi-region, multi-account hybrid cloud deployments where flexible centralized routing is required. Pairing DX Gateway with Transit Gateway means use transit gateway attached to a direct connect gateway to enable scalable inter-vpc routing and full hybrid reachability.. In practical terms, how transit gateway extends dx gateway capabilities for global routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Extension
keyIdea.text: Use Transit Gateway attached to a Direct Connect Gateway to enable scalable inter-VPC routing and full hybrid reachability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › DX Gateway + Transit Gateway
Why pair with TGW

TGW provides the routing plane for VPC-to-VPC communication and centralized route management across regions.

Attach TGW to DX Gateway using a Transit VIF.
Use TGW route tables to manage which VPCs and attachments are reachable from on-premises.
Enable route propagation for attachments that must receive on-premises routes.
Operational checklist
  • Create Transit VIF to attach TGW to DX Gateway.
  • Verify TGW route tables and propagation settings.
  • Confirm on-premises route table learns VPC prefixes managed by TGW.
Key Takeaway

Pairing DX Gateway with TGW creates a scalable global hub that supports inter-VPC routing and hybrid connectivity.

screens.title: Scenario: Connect VPCs in two regions from one Direct Connect
screens.subtitle: Conceptual steps and routing review for a two-region example

narration.text: Let's walk through a hands-on scenario conceptualized in the chapter. Your company has VPCs in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, and a single Direct Connect connection in us-east-1. The task is to let on-premises reach both VPCs via a Direct Connect Gateway. Step one: create the Direct Connect Gateway in us-east-1 and choose an Amazon-side ASN. Step two: create and attach a VGW to the VPC in us-east-1. Step three: create and attach a VGW to the VPC in eu-west-1. Step four: associate both VGWs with the Direct Connect Gateway. After associations, validate that your on-premises router learns both VPC CIDRs through BGP and that each VPC route table points to its VGW for on-premises prefixes. Answer the key conceptual questions: your on-premises router learns both VPC routes via BGP from the DX Gateway; VPC route tables need explicit entries pointing back to VGW or TGW so return traffic goes to on-premises; and VPCs in the two regions will not communicate through the DX Gateway because transitive routing is not supported. If inter-VPC communication is required, use a Transit Gateway or VPC peering as the next design step.

Question

How will on-premises learn both VPCs' routes? Via BGP advertisements from the DX Gateway after association.

Question

What route table changes are needed? Each VPC route table must route on-premises prefixes to its VGW or TGW.

Question

Can VPCs communicate directly via DX Gateway? No — Direct Connect Gateway does not support transitive VPC-to-VPC routing.

screens.title: Common configuration mistakes and checks
screens.subtitle: Practical pitfalls: missing attachments, wrong ASNs, and route table errors

narration.text: Successful DX Gateway deployments require careful verification to avoid frequent mistakes. One common error is attempting to associate a VGW before it has been attached to its VPC — the association will fail. Another is misconfiguring BGP by using an Amazon-side ASN that collides with your on-premises ASN policies or forgetting to allow the ASN in routing policies. Route table omissions are also frequent: teams configure BGP and the DX Gateway but forget to add VPC route table entries that direct on-premises prefixes to the VGW or TGW. Overlapping CIDRs cause hard-to-debug routing conflicts and must be resolved at the addressing plan level. Finally, assuming the Direct Connect Gateway will provide transitive inter-VPC routing is a design mistake; if you need that connectivity use a Transit Gateway attached to the DX Gateway. To reduce risk, use a pre-deployment checklist: verify attachments, confirm ASN choices, run BGP adjacency checks, review learned routes, and validate VPC route tables. These checks prevent downtime and ensure predictable routing behavior across a global hybrid network. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the core concepts to remember. First, a Direct Connect Gateway is a global resource that centralizes hybrid connectivity so one Direct Connect connection can reach multiple VPCs in different regions by associating their VGWs or TGWs. Second, a VGW association requires the VGW to be attached to its VPC before association, and a TGW must have VPC attachments prior to association as well. Third, the Amazon-side ASN you choose for the Direct Connect Gateway is used for BGP peering with your on-premises router and must be planned to avoid conflicts. Keep these points in mind when designing multi-region hybrid networks and use them as checkpoints when you configure the environment. screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three concise reminders for design and operations

narration.text: Three concise reminders to keep close as you design hybrid global networks. First, do not allow overlapping CIDRs across VPCs or between on-premises and VPCs — overlaps break deterministic routing. Second, Direct Connect Gateways do not support transitive routing between associated VGWs; plan TGW attachments if inter-VPC routing is required. Third, always validate attachments and BGP: ensure VGW or TGW attachments exist, choose a non-conflicting Amazon-side ASN, confirm BGP adjacency, and verify that VPC route tables contain return routes for on-premises prefixes. These checks prevent outages and ensure predictable connectivity. Keep this checklist for every DX Gateway deployment.
